IN BUDGET — WELL UNDERGROUND FLOOR — ALL ON ONE LEVELOWNS THE FREEHOLD TO THE BUILDING199-YEAR LEASE FROM 2018OWN GOOD-SIZED REAR GARDENLEVEL WALK TO TOWN, STATION & SEAFRONTON-STREET PARKING ONLY (residents’ permit zone)
🅿️ On-street parking only — No off-road parking is claimed anywhere on the listing. The front is a small gravelled forecourt behind a low brick wall with a path to the door — there is no dropped kerb visible in the photos, so do not assume you could park a car on it without applying for one. Researching the street: Devon County Council’s 2023 Exmouth traffic orders put ‘No Waiting At Any Time’ on specified lengths of Lyndhurst Road, and a later amendment order proposes Residents Parking (Zonal), 8am–8pm, Zone D on specified lengths of the same road. So a resident permit looks obtainable, but which side and which stretch matters a lot here — ask Devon County Council (or the agent) exactly which length of Lyndhurst Road this address falls on before assuming a permit gets you a space near the door. As a fallback, East Devon District Council sells a virtual monthly town permit valid in its Exmouth pay-and-display car parks, and Phear Park is a couple of minutes away.

📐 Floor plan
Open full Google Maps ↗ Directions ↗

A bay-fronted Edwardian terrace on Lyndhurst Road, split into two flats, with this one occupying the whole ground floor. Accommodation is an entrance hall, a bay-fronted sitting room that doubles as bedroom 2 (17ft into the bay), a separate living/dining room, fitted kitchen, lean-to utility, master bedroom and a bathroom with shower over the bath. Gas central heating and uPVC double glazing throughout. Outside there is a good-sized enclosed rear garden — shingle by the house, then lawn, a raised artificial-grass deck, shrub borders, brick and timber-fenced boundaries and a pedestrian gate to the rear. The unusual bit is the tenure: the flat is leasehold on a 199-year lease granted 31 January 2018, but it also owns the freehold of the whole building, which contains just one other flat on the first floor. In practice that means you control the building rather than answering to a landlord or a managing agent.

Why it's here: Sub-£200k, genuinely all on one level, with its own private garden and effective control of the freehold — that combination almost never appears at this price around Exmouth. It is a level walk to the town centre, the railway station and Phear Park, and the seafront is a manageable stroll. The Edwardian bay and brick frontage give it more character than most flats on the list. The catch is parking: nothing off-road, and Lyndhurst Road sits inside Exmouth’s residents’ permit machinery, so that is the thing to pin down before offering.

🤖 AI's take: Cheap, entirely ground-floor, with its own garden and effective ownership of the building — the only real gap is off-road parking.

Researching it: Devon County Council’s 2023 Exmouth parking orders put ‘No Waiting At Any Time’ on specified lengths of Clinton Square itself, so the kerb directly outside is likely to be restricted rather than a free-for-all. The surrounding central streets fall inside Exmouth’s residents’ parking zones (introduced 2023, now five zones with resident, visitor, business and blue-badge permit types), so a resident permit is the realistic route — but this is the busiest, most tourist-pressured part of town in summer and a permit gives priority, not a reserved bay. Researching Ottery: Devon County Council has not introduced a residents’ permit scheme here, so unrestricted on-street stretches are simply first-come-first-served — better than a permit lottery in some ways, worse in that you have no priority at all. East Devon District Council’s Brook Street car park is in the centre of town a few minutes’ walk away (charges 08:00–18:00 Monday–Saturday, from 50p for 30 minutes, free on Sundays), and EDDC’s virtual monthly town permit covers Ottery St Mary for its car parks. The Sainsbury’s car park on Hind Street also offers monthly parking from around £65. A brick-and-flint mid-terrace cottage fronting straight onto the pavement on North Street, within walking distance of Ottery St Mary town centre and inside the King’s School catchment. Downstairs is a large sitting/dining room with exposed beams and an exposed timber floor, a timber window seat, and a brick fireplace housing a log burner; the kitchen opens onto a covered veranda. Upstairs are two bedrooms and a family bathroom — the front bedroom has a cast-iron fireplace and original stripped-pine cupboard doors. The garden is the headline: Hall & Scott describe it as one of the largest in the area, with a good-sized paved patio, a small deck with a whitewashed wall surround, and lawn with flower borders. At the far end is a studio (2.9m x 2.2m) with light and power laid on, opening onto its own decked patio. Chain-free.

Why it's here: This is the sort of thing Bro 3 has rated well before — real character, a genuinely finished outbuilding that could work as a studio or guest space, and a garden well out of proportion to the price. The exposed beams, timber floor and working log burner are the real deal rather than a stripped-back modernisation. The downsides, plainly: it is inland, so the coast checklist item is a straight no, and it fronts the pavement with no parking mentioned anywhere. Ottery is roughly 25 minutes from Exmouth and closer to the Otterton side, so it is a compromise on location rather than a disqualification.

🤖 AI's take: Genuine cottage character, a log burner and an outsized garden with a finished studio — undercut by being inland with no parking and no realistic ground-floor bedroom.

A spacious ground-floor apartment in Redcliff Court, reached by the drive immediately before The Rosemullion Apartments on Cliff Road. Share of freehold, no chain, all on one level, and coast path access straight off the communal grounds. A three-bedroom freehold terrace on Gibson Close, a quiet residential cul-de-sac in Exmouth. Entrance porch into a 15ft 8in x 13ft 2in lounge with the staircase rising from it, then a 15ft 8in kitchen/dining room fitted with a gas hob and built-in oven, running the full depth of the house with double doors opening onto the rear garden. Upstairs are three bedrooms — the main with a fitted wardrobe range and dressing table — and a bathroom/WC with shower over the bath and a heated towel rail. Double glazing, gas central heating and solar panels already installed. Front garden with a path and an outside store; the rear garden is the best bit, sunny and well screened, laid to lawn with a patio, stocked flower and shrub beds, a shed and an outside tap. A garage sits in a block close by.

Why it's here: Three bedrooms, freehold, a garage and solar panels for under £270,000 is solid value in Exmouth, and the secluded sunny rear garden lifts it above the usual terrace. It is an ordinary modern house rather than anything characterful, which is where Bro 3 has consistently marked things down, and the garage being in a block rather than on the plot means day-to-day parking outside the door is still on-street in the close — worth checking how crowded that gets.

🤖 AI's take: Three freehold bedrooms, a garage, solar and a genuinely nice private garden — sensible value, but a plain modern house with no character to speak of.

An immaculate modern two-bedroom corner link house on Brackendale, in the Brixington area of north Exmouth. Ground floor is an entrance hall with a run of storage cupboards, a bay-fronted living room and a contemporary fitted kitchen with integrated electric oven, induction hob, washer/dryer and slimline dishwasher; upstairs are two well-proportioned bedrooms and a bathroom with a Mira electric shower over the bath. Double glazed and gas centrally heated, with a combi boiler fitted in January 2026. Outside there is a small enclosed garden laid to stone chippings with timber fencing, and two allocated parking spaces immediately in front of the property. Freehold, with a service charge noted on the particulars for the estate’s communal areas.

Why it's here: Two allocated parking spaces on a freehold house at £230,000 is a genuinely good practical package, and it needs nothing doing — the boiler is eight months old and the kitchen is current. A sensible fallback, not a find.

🤖 AI's take: Freehold, two parking spaces and nothing to do to it — but a characterless modern box with a chippings yard, on the wrong edge of town for the sea.

A ground-floor two-bedroom apartment at 52 Norman Crescent, Budleigh Salterton (EX9 6RB), guide £192,000 with Red Homes and no chain. Communal doors front and rear with an entry phone lead to a private hallway. The lounge is 4.77m x 3.66m and bright with double-glazed windows, with a fitted kitchen of 3.55m x 1.63m alongside — inset sink, electric hob with extractor, fitted oven and space for freestanding appliances. The principal bedroom is a 3.55m x 2.72m double with its own en-suite shower room, and the second bedroom, 2.56m x 2.72m, has two built-in cupboards and would suit a guest room or office. There is a separate family bathroom with a panelled bath. Heating is by night storage and electric wall heaters rather than gas. Outside, the flat comes with one allocated parking space and residents share a well-managed gated lawned garden. Tenure is leasehold on a 155-year lease from 2003, so roughly 132 years remain — ground rent £167.71 per half year, service and management £453.07 per half year, and buildings insurance £261.96 a year, giving total outgoings of about £1,500 a year. Council tax band B, EPC C.

Why it's here: This is the cheapest thing on the list that is genuinely ground-floor, has its own allocated parking, and gives two bedrooms and two bathrooms — at £192,000 it sits close to the real £170k target rather than the £300k ceiling. Budleigh puts it near the Otterton brother and an easy run to Exmouth. The trade-offs are that it is leasehold, and while 132 years is a comfortable term, roughly £1,500 a year of combined service charge, ground rent and insurance is a standing cost a freehold house would not carry; there is also no private garden, only the shared gated lawn, and no character in a 2003 block.

🤖 AI's take: Cheap, genuinely ground-floor, two beds and two bathrooms with its own parking space in Budleigh — the closest thing here to the real £170k target, docked for leasehold, ~£1,500/yr outgoings and no private garden or character.

A one-double-bedroom semi-detached bungalow tucked into a quiet cul-de-sac off Ashleigh Road on the edge of Exmouth, guide £225,000 freehold with Links, no onward chain. The layout is a single open-plan living room/kitchen of 17ft4 x 15ft2 with a breakfast bar, built-in electric hob and oven, and a window to the rear looking over the garden with Phear Park beyond. Off it is a 12ft5 x 9ft8 uPVC conservatory with French doors to the garden and views over Exmouth, a 13ft11 x 11ft6 double bedroom to the front, and a dual-aspect bathroom of 10ft7 x 5ft5 fitted with a four-piece suite including both a bath and a separate triple shower tray with a rainfall thermostatic shower. Gas central heating via a combi boiler, uPVC double glazing throughout, and solar panels are already fitted with the control unit indoors. The loft is insulated and part-boarded with its own double-glazed window, and the agent notes it could be converted for further accommodation subject to the usual consents. Outside is a driveway to the front leading to a detached garage, and a good-sized enclosed rear garden arranged over terraces. Council tax band B, about 452 sq ft.

Why it's here: For the long-term brief this is one of the better shapes on the list — a genuine bungalow, so everything that matters is on one level, with a driveway, a detached garage for a workshop, a garden with a view over Phear Park, and solar panels already paid for by somebody else. The loft with a window and conversion potential is real upside on a small footprint. The obvious limit is that it is a one-bedroom house at 452 sq ft, so it works as a home for one but has no room for guests without converting that loft, and there are steps up from the driveway to the front door.

🤖 AI's take: A true one-level bungalow with driveway, detached garage, terraced garden, park views and solar panels already fitted — strong on the things that matter long-term, held back by being a single bedroom at 452 sq ft with no real character.

🤖 AI's take: Listed Georgian character, 860 sq ft, sea views and a private front garden two minutes from Exmouth beach at £250,000, with a 999-year lease and share of freehold that neutralises most leasehold objections — docked for having no parking, needing modernisation, and being reached down external steps.

Research findings

Asked: What are the realistic parking options for a flat on Louisa Terrace with no allocated space? (2026-08-16)

Devon County Council approved a residents' and business parking permit scheme for Exmouth after a consultation showing strong support, and three residents' parking zones went live in 2023, with a further consultation in late 2024 on adding zones in the Withycombe Road and Carter Avenue areas. Permits are administered digitally through MiPermit, with a first residents' permit costing roughly £35 a year for a band A vehicle and higher rates for additional permits and higher-emission vehicles. Louisa Terrace appears in Devon's MiPermit street listings, which indicates on-street controls apply there. The zones were drawn street by street rather than blanket-covering the town centre, so the specific zone and eligibility for this address should be checked directly against Devon CC's Exmouth traffic regulation orders before relying on it.

Sources: Devon County Council — Exmouth residents parking · MiPermit Devon — permit purchase · Exmouth Journal — residents' parking permit scheme approved

A purpose-built ground-floor two-bedroom apartment in the "Avenues" area of Exmouth, guide £280,000–£300,000 through Your Move, reduced on 11/08/2026 and described as a motivated seller with no ongoing chain. Entry is via a security door with remote unlocking into a hallway with ample storage and a utility cupboard plumbed for a washing machine, with space for a tumble dryer and the manifold for the underfloor heating. The main room is a large open-plan lounge/dining area with a modern integrated kitchen and French doors opening onto its own planted patio. Both bedrooms are doubles and both have their own white en-suite shower rooms, and there is a further cloakroom/WC. Outside are maintained communal gardens, a communal bin store and a secure shared shed with an individual lockable unit per flat. Parking is an allocated space inside a secure residents’ area behind remote-controlled gates onto Elwyn Road. Tenure is share of freehold on a 125-year lease running from 24 February 2011 (about 110 years remaining); the service charge is 6.6% of the annual budget, currently around £157 a month or £1,892.81 a year, covering buildings insurance and all communal areas. Exmouth station is 0.84 miles away.

Why it's here: Of everything on this list, this is one of the very few that answers the "what if stairs stop being an option" question outright rather than theoretically — it is genuinely ground floor, level throughout, with its own patio via French doors and a gated allocated parking space a few steps away. Two double bedrooms each with their own en-suite is unusual at this price and makes it work properly for guests or family staying. The Avenues is a good part of Exmouth, under a mile from the station and walkable to the seafront. The reservations are the money. £280,000 is not cheap for a flat, the £1,893 annual service charge is a real ongoing cost on top, and it is a modern purpose-built block with no character whatsoever — the opposite end of the spectrum from the thatched cottages Jesse actually gravitates towards. The share of freehold and the 110-year lease are both reassuring, and the seller being motivated after a reduction is worth testing with an offer.

🤖 AI's take: The most genuinely step-free option on the list — ground floor, own patio, gated allocated parking, two en-suites and share of freehold — but £280,000 with a £1,893 service charge for a modern block with no character is a lot of money for very little soul.

A two-double-bedroom end-of-terrace house on Vansittart Drive, guide £255,000 through Links Estate Agents, added on 11/08/2026 and the newest Exmouth listing in this sweep. Downstairs is a modern fitted cloakroom, a living room and an impressive kitchen/breakfast room with a granite breakfast bar; upstairs are two good-sized doubles, the principal with a large built-in wardrobe, plus a modern bathroom. Gas central heating and uPVC double glazing throughout. Outside there is a brick paved driveway giving off-road parking, an enclosed low-maintenance rear garden, a sun room/conservatory and — the feature Links push hardest — a garden room they suggest would work as a home office or hobby room. Freehold, council tax band B, no onward chain. Exmouth station is 1.6 miles away. This is a different property from the £249,950 Vansittart Drive house already on the list, and from the £290,000 one currently marketed by Your Move on the same road.

Why it's here: The garden room is the reason to look twice. Jesse has consistently rated separate, finished outbuildings — workshop, studio, bike space — as a genuine plus rather than a nice-to-have, and Bro 3 said the same explicitly about the sheds at Haynes Cottages. Here you get one, plus a sun room, plus a driveway, plus a downstairs cloakroom that makes a future ground-floor adaptation considerably easier, all freehold and chain-free at £255,000. Against that: it is an unremarkable modern end-terrace with no character at all, in a residential pocket a mile and a half back from both the station and the seafront, and £255,000 is £85,000 above Jesse’s real target. It is the practical option rather than the interesting one — but it does the practical things properly.

🅿️ On-street parking only — No off-road parking is mentioned anywhere on the listing, so this is kerbside only. The useful part is that Egremont Road falls inside the Exmouth residents’ parking permit scheme — Devon County Council approved it after consultation, and Egremont Road is named within the "colonies" area (Zone A), one of five Exmouth zones with resident, visitor, essential visitor, business, trade and blue badge permit types. A resident permit therefore gives priority to park in the immediate area, which is a real improvement on unrestricted free-for-all streets, but it is not a reserved bay and it is not a guaranteed space — demand near the station is high. Check the current permit cost and the household allocation limit with Devon County Council, and note that the rear access shown on the floorplan is pedestrian, not vehicular.

A three-bedroom freehold terraced house on Egremont Road, guide £265,000 through Bradleys, added on 07/08/2026 and offered with no onward chain. The floorplan totals 896 sq ft over two floors, split almost exactly evenly: downstairs a lounge (11’8" x 10’8") with a feature fireplace, a separate dining room (13’1" x 11’8") and a 12’7" x 8’0" kitchen at the back; upstairs two doubles (12’5" x 10’8" and 13’1" x 9’5"), a small third bedroom (8’0" x 6’2") and the bathroom. Bradleys highlight the high ceilings and the feature fireplace as the character draw. Outside is an enclosed rear garden with a patio, lawn, shed and rear access. What stands out on the map is the location: Exmouth station is 0.22 miles away, which is about a four-minute walk, and the seafront and town centre are a similar distance in the other direction.

Why it's here: Three bedrooms, freehold, period features and a garden, four minutes from the train station and about the same from the town centre, for £265,000 — on paper this is one of the better-value Exmouth houses to appear in a while, and it is the closest to a station of anything currently on the list. The high ceilings and fireplace give it more character than the usual Exmouth terrace, and the third bedroom, small as it is, makes it genuinely flexible. The problem is parking. Bradleys do not mention any, which on a road of this type means kerbside only, and Egremont Road sits inside the Exmouth residents’ permit zone — so a permit is likely available but a guaranteed space is not. Parking is a hard requirement for an ordinary house in this search, and this is an ordinary house. Weigh the station and the price against the near-certainty of circling the block on a summer evening.

🤖 AI's take: A genuinely well-located three-bed freehold with period features, a garden and the station four minutes away at a fair price — held back only by having no parking at all beyond a residents’ permit.

The floorplan runs to 57.5 sq m (619 sq ft) on a single level: a hall with a useful entrance storage cupboard, a separate living room (14’8" x 9’2"), a 15’1" x 8’2" kitchen, two bedrooms (14’8" x 9’0" and 10’10" x 8’1") and a bathroom positioned between them. Tenure is leasehold with the lease running to 28/09/2130 — about 105 years remaining — and Rightmove reports no ground rent and no service charge review period, with the actual service charge figure not published on the listing. Why it's here: This is one of the cheapest ways into Budleigh Salterton town centre that has appeared in months, and at £175,000 it sits close to Jesse’s real £170k target rather than the £300k ceiling. Everything is on one level, which is exactly the long-term shape he has said he wants, and the High Street position puts the pebble beach, the Jurassic Coast path and the whole run of independent shops within a few minutes on foot. There is no parking at all — Budleigh’s High Street has only limited, restricted on-street bays, so this would mean paying for a car park permit indefinitely. 🤖 AI's take: Cheap for central Budleigh, chain-free, and entirely on one level — but no parking, no garden, no outside space at all, and the listing never says which floor it is on, which undercuts the one thing that would otherwise make it stand out.

The ground floor is a single dual-aspect lounge/dining room of 15'8" x 15'6" (narrowing to 9'2") with windows to front and side, running through to a compact 8'0" x 6'8" kitchen with a wall-mounted gas boiler and a door out to the rear. Double glazed, gas central heating, EPC C. Update 18/08/2026: now being sold by traditional online auction with Pennys on 4 September 2026 at 11.30am, rather than by private treaty — the £150,000 figure is effectively a guide, and the sitting tenant at £870pcm remains in place.

Why it's here: £150,000 for a freehold semi-detached house in Exmouth is the cheapest house — not flat, house — the sweep has turned up in central Exmouth, and it is barely a ten-minute walk from the town centre and Exmouth Community College. Worth putting in front of the brothers precisely because the price is so far below everything else on the page.

Why it's here: On paper this is one of the better-value things on the whole page. £155,000 buys a genuinely ground-floor two-double-bedroom home half a mile from the beach in Budleigh, with its own private enclosed garden and a lockable store — not a shared communal lawn, an actual garden — plus a nearly-new boiler and windows, so nothing needs spending on day one. It answers the long-term stairs question completely, and the lease is a comfortable 99 years with a trivial £10 ground rent and a £224 service charge. Two things need eyes on before getting excited. Second, it is a modern-method auction, so there is a non-refundable reservation fee on top of the guide and a fixed timetable once reserved. Parking is kerbside only. A ground-floor two-double-bedroom apartment on Cranford Avenue, reached by its own private front door off the communal hallway. The rooms are generous for the price: a 15'11" x 12'3" lounge/dining room with a door onto a covered sun terrace that opens directly onto the communal gardens, an 11'3" kitchen, a 16'7" principal bedroom and an 11' second bedroom, both with fitted floor-to-ceiling wardrobes, plus a bathroom/WC. A single garage in a nearby block with an up-and-over door comes with it, and the development has extensive, well-maintained communal lawns and mature planting front and rear. Two things explain the £150,000 asking price, and Pennys are upfront about both: the flat needs a full programme of modernisation and refurbishment, and — in their words — "price reflects length of lease". The lease is 99 years from 1969, so roughly 42 years remain. Service charge is £1,530.87 for 2025 (revised annually) and ground rent is £10 every six months.

Why it's here: On the face of it this hits several things at once that rarely come together: genuinely cheap, explicitly ground floor with no internal stairs at all, two proper double bedrooms rather than a double and a box room, its own garage, and mature communal gardens right outside the sun terrace. For the "could still live here if stairs became a problem" test it is the strongest kind of answer — it is already all on one level. The problem is the lease, and it is a serious one rather than a technicality. At around 42 years remaining it is well under the 80-year mark where marriage value kicks in, which means most mainstream lenders will not touch it without an extension, and extending will cost a meaningful five-figure sum on top of the purchase price and legal fees. Add a full refurbishment and a £1,531 annual service charge and the true all-in cost lands a long way above the £150,000 headline — quite possibly north of £220,000 for a flat with no character. Worth a conversation with the agent about whether the freeholder will grant an extension and at what price, because that single answer decides whether this is a bargain or a trap. Bro 3 has already said he is wary of anything not comfortably over 100 years, so expect a low score from him.

🤖 AI's take: Cheap, properly all-on-one-level, two real doubles and its own garage — but a ~42-year lease puts it below the mortgageable threshold and the extension plus a full refurbishment would push the true cost far past the £150,000 headline.

Why it's here: This is the most turn-key thing in the search right now: freehold, three bedrooms, fully modernised so there is nothing that has to be done on day one, and parking sorted twice over with both an integrated garage and off-road space at the front. Woodbury Common is handy from this side of Exmouth and both brothers are a short drive away. It scores as a sensible option rather than an exciting one.

🤖 AI's take: Freehold, fully modernised, three bedrooms, off-road parking plus an integrated garage already wired and plumbed as a workshop — practically the strongest package here, marked down for having no character and sitting near the top of the budget.

Freehold parcels of land, each about a third of an acre (roughly 13,000 sq ft / 1,208 sq m), on the Exmouth Road between the villages of Ebford and Exton, offered by auction with a £30,000 guide. The listing describes a prominent roadside position with established vehicle access. Critically, this is bare land with no planning permission — the agent markets it as "ideal for a variety of uses subject to the necessary consents" and it carries a 30% planning overage, meaning if residential or other valuable consent is ever obtained, 30% of the resulting uplift in value is payable back to the seller. Reserve is set within the guide range or no more than 10% above it, and the usual auction fees apply on top. Came to market 2 August 2026. Update 18/08/2026: the auction date is now confirmed — the individual parcels (Plots C and D, each about 0.3 acres, EX3 0PQ) are listed by Auction House South West for National Online Auction starting 1 September 2026 and ending 2 September 2026, each at a £30,000 guide plus fees, still freehold and still subject to the planning overage.

Why it's here: Worth tracking because it is cheap, genuinely unconventional, and in a spot that suits Jesse well on paper — the Ebford/Exton stretch sits right by the Exe estuary with Exton station on the Avocet line, ten minutes from Exmouth and very close to the Woodbury brother, with Woodbury Common trails a short ride away. At £30,000 the downside is small in absolute terms. But it should be read as a speculative punt rather than a route to a home, and the reasons are stacked up in the listing itself. There is no planning permission of any kind, this is open countryside outside any settlement boundary, and East Devon is not in the habit of granting new isolated dwellings there. The 30% overage clause is the clearest signal of all: the seller has priced in the possibility that a buyer tries for consent, and has arranged to take almost a third of the gain if it ever lands. Note also that Plot B on the same stretch of Exmouth Road, tracked here separately, went to auction on 3 August 2026 with a £75,000 guide and its listing has now been pulled — so this may well be the same land being re-marketed at a lower guide, which is a fact worth establishing with the agent before bidding.

🤖 AI's take: A third of an acre with its own road access, ten minutes from Exmouth and next to Woodbury Common, for £30,000 — but it is bare countryside with no planning permission and a 30% overage clause, so it is a cheap speculative punt on consent rather than anywhere to live.

A freehold two-bedroom semi-detached bungalow on the eastern outskirts of Ottery St Mary at £250,000, a level walk from the town centre. Accommodation is a reception porch and hall, a fully fitted kitchen with built-in oven and gas hob and slate-effect worktops, a sitting/dining room with a large picture window and a feature fireplace, two double bedrooms both with built-in wardrobes, and a modern shower room. uPVC double glazing throughout, gas central heating and a new gas boiler. Why it's here: This is the most straightforwardly practical entry of the batch and it ticks the two boxes that are hardest to find together: it is a bungalow, so the stay-put-if-stairs-become-a-problem question is answered outright rather than as an adaptation, and the garage has light, power and a utility area, which makes it a usable workspace rather than just somewhere to put a car. Add a driveway on top, a new boiler, an enclosed low-maintenance garden and a shed with home-office potential, and there is very little that would need spending on straight away. The case against is the one Jesse and Bro 3 both apply hardest. There is no character here — it is a mid-century estate bungalow, competently presented, with nothing unusual about it — and Ottery St Mary is properly inland, roughly 25 minutes from the nearest sea and about the same again from Exmouth, so it fails both the ocean and the close-to-family tests. At £250,000 for two bedrooms it also sits in exactly the zone where Bro 3 has repeatedly said a place feels expensive for what it is.

🤖 AI's take: Ticks the practical boxes cleanly — a true bungalow, a driveway, and a garage with power and a utility that would actually work as a workshop — but it has no character at all and sits inland, well away from both the sea and either brother.

A freehold single building plot of about 0.126 acres (0.05 ha) on the north-western edge of Sidmouth, north of Woolbrook Mead and close to the Waitrose. Detailed — not outline — planning permission was granted by East Devon District Council under reference 23/2134/FUL on 5 February 2024 for the construction of one new detached dwelling and associated works. The approved design is a three-bedroom dormer-style house of roughly 191 sq m (2,063 sq ft): ground floor gives an entrance hall, an en-suite bedroom, utility, WC and an open-plan kitchen/living/dining room opening onto the garden; the upper floor adds two large bedrooms, both en-suite with built-in wardrobes. Off-road parking is shown at the front, accessed from Core Hill Road, with an established westerly-facing garden to the rear. The lead photo is an aerial with the plot boundary drawn on it, which places it clearly in an established residential area with the sea visible in the distance.

Why it's here: Jesse has asked repeatedly for self-build plots to be surfaced, and this is the strongest version of that this sweep found: the hard planning risk is already retired, because permission is detailed rather than outline and covers a specific approved house, so a buyer is not gambling on whether East Devon will ever allow a dwelling here. The approved layout is also unusually well-suited to him without needing any redesign — there is a full en-suite bedroom, utility and WC on the ground floor alongside the living space, which is the ground-floor-forever box ticked from day one rather than as a later adaptation. Two real caveats. First, £220,000 buys the land only; a 191 sq m house will realistically cost well north of £250,000 to build, so the all-in figure lands far above the £300,000 ceiling even though the listing price sits under it. Second, a February 2024 detailed consent carries the standard three-year commencement window, so it expires around February 2027 unless work has lawfully started — worth confirming with EDDC before doing anything else. Location-wise Sidmouth is about 30 minutes from Exmouth and 20 from Otterton, so it is the weakest of this batch on closeness to family, and there is no railway station in the town at all.

🤖 AI's take: The self-build option Jesse keeps asking for, with detailed planning already granted and a ground-floor en-suite bedroom in the approved layout — but £220,000 is the land alone, and the build cost on top pushes the real total well past the ceiling, in a town that is the furthest of this batch from both brothers.

Researching it: Talaton has no residents' permit scheme and no council car park at all — Devon County Council handles on-street parking countywide and East Devon District Council's car parks are all in the towns (Ottery St Mary, Honiton, Budleigh, Exmouth), none in the village. In practice that means unrestricted on-street/verge parking on the lanes around the green, plus the church and village hall car parks which are informally used by residents. That is usually workable in a village this small, but it is not guaranteed and it is not the same as owning a space — worth asking Redferns directly whether the cottage has any recognised parking right, because for a listed cottage in a conservation-sensitive village there is no realistic prospect of creating a driveway.

A properly thatched Grade II listed cottage in the middle of Talaton, a few steps from the village green, offered with no onward chain. Ground floor: a cosy sitting room with a striking stone inglenook fireplace, a leaded-light window with a window seat and an abundance of exposed ceiling beams; a kitchen with wall and base units, built-in oven, hob and extractor and an integrated washing machine; and a couple of steps down to a dining area with wooden flooring and more beams, which opens directly into Bedroom Two and on to a rear porch and the garden. First floor: the principal bedroom with built-in storage, plus the bathroom. Heating is electric storage heaters — mains gas is not connected. Council Tax Band C, freehold, EPC-exempt as a listed building. Outside there is a rear garden mostly laid to lawn with a flowerbed and a summerhouse; separately, the current owner and the neighbours rent an adjoining strip of garden land from a local landowner for a modest annual sum, and the landowner has indicated they are happy for that to continue — worth confirming in writing, since it is rented rather than owned. The village itself has a community-run shop and post office, a pub, an active village hall and a medieval parish church; Ottery St Mary is 3 miles away, Honiton 5 miles with a train station, and the A30 is close for Exeter and the M5.

Why it's here: This is the best straight-up thatched cottage the sweep has turned up in budget for a while — genuinely thatched, genuinely Grade II, freehold, chain-free, with a stone inglenook, beams throughout and a garden with a summerhouse, all at £245,000 rather than the £385,000–£450,000 the East Budleigh and Castle Lane thatched cottages want. It also gives Jesse a downstairs room already being used as a bedroom. The honest trade-off is geography: Talaton is inland, about 25 minutes from the Budleigh/Sidmouth coast and roughly 20 minutes from both brothers rather than the few miles the East Budleigh options manage, and it has no parking of its own. Electric storage heating and the rented garden strip are two more things to price in.

🤖 AI's take: A real thatched Grade II cottage — inglenook, beams, summerhouse garden, freehold and chain-free — at £245,000, which is a lot of character per pound; it loses points for being genuinely inland (no sea, ~20 minutes from either brother) and for having no parking of its own.

❓ Parking unclear — The listing makes no mention of parking at all — no allocated space, garage or driveway is claimed, and the photos don't show one. Researching the street specifically: Station Road is where East Devon District Council's Lower Station Road car park sits, effectively on the doorstep, and EDDC's published rules give it no restriction of use at all between 1 October and 31 March, which makes winter parking straightforward and free. Outside that window it is a paid short-stay car park, but EDDC sells virtual monthly permits at £10/month for one town (Budleigh Salterton is one of the eligible towns), rising in £2 steps if you want to add more towns, with no physical permit to display. So the realistic position is: no parking with the flat, but a council car park within yards of the front door and a cheap monthly permit that covers it — a better fallback than most of the no-parking cottages on this list. Still worth asking David Rhys & Co whether any of the building's residents have an informal arrangement, because a converted Edwardian town house of this size often has some rear access.

A spacious ground-floor apartment forming part of a distinctive Edwardian town house on Station Road, right beside The Green in Budleigh Salterton. 796 sq ft on one level: lounge/diner, kitchen/breakfast room, two double bedrooms, bathroom, and generous storage throughout. The agent's line is that the building has "managed to retain a great deal of character and charm", and the conversion has kept the period proportions rather than chopping them up. There is a communal front garden included. EPC C. Tenure is a share of freehold, to be created on completion — so the exact lease length isn't stated yet and needs pinning down with the solicitor. Pets and lettings are both permitted. Notably it is available for the first time in 21 years. Walking distance to the town's shops, the seafront and the bus routes; Exmouth and its train station are about five miles away.

Why it's here: On paper this ticks more of Jesse's actual long-term boxes than almost anything else at this price: it is fully ground floor with two double bedrooms, so the "could I still live here if I couldn't manage stairs" test is already passed rather than merely adaptable; it is in Budleigh Salterton a few minutes' walk from the sea; it is a period conversion rather than a modern box; and at £189,950 it sits below Jesse's real £170k–£200k comfort zone rather than at the £300k ceiling. It is also close to both brothers — Otterton is about three miles, Woodbury about six. The gaps are parking, which the listing simply doesn't address, and the share-of-freehold structure needing proper legal checking because the lease is only being created at completion.

🤖 AI's take: Fully ground-floor, two doubles, period character, five minutes from the Budleigh seafront and close to both brothers, at £189,950 — the ground-floor-for-life test is passed outright; the catches are no parking of its own (though the council car park is on the same street) and a share-of-freehold lease that only gets written at completion.

A two-bedroom mid-terrace cottage in the hamlet of Alfington, offered with no onward chain at a £185,000 guide. Ground floor: a lounge with a feature fireplace and wood-burning fire, a separate dining room, and a kitchen with base units and built-in appliances. First floor: two bedrooms and a shower room. Described by the agent as beautifully presented. Crucially for this list it has genuine off-road parking — a 4.18m x 2.58m carport — which almost nothing else at this price in a village setting does. Rear access leads to a brick-paved patio and an artificial-lawned garden with a pergola, all landscaped. Two practical caveats stated in the listing: heating is night storage heaters, not gas central heating, and drainage is shared private drainage rather than mains. The front elevation is rendered and fronts straight onto the lane, and the render on the plinth looks tired in the photos even though the interior is smart. Alfington sits just outside Ottery St Mary with A30 access and a bus service.

Why it's here: It is one of the cheapest genuinely rural, genuinely characterful cottages the sweep has found that also comes with its own off-road parking — that combination is rare enough to be worth tracking on its own. At £185,000 it lands inside Jesse's real target range rather than near the ceiling, it is chain-free, and Alfington is properly small and quiet, which suits the stated preference for somewhere more remote than a village centre. Against it: night storage heating and shared private drainage are both cost and hassle items that will show up on any survey, there is no sea within reach (Sidmouth is roughly 25 minutes), and it is about 20 minutes from each brother rather than the few miles the East Budleigh and Budleigh options manage.

🤖 AI's take: Cheap, chain-free, quiet and — unusually for a village cottage at this price — it has its own carport, which is why it earns its place; it is held back by being properly inland with no coast and no brother nearby, plus night storage heating and shared private drainage to price in.

Research findings

Asked: Please do a deep dive: the roof looks a little bad on the back. Would love to find out about parking on this street — seems strangely empty in the photos but no off-street parking shown, what do they do? Also what's behind it — if I have my bike in the shed can I take it out of the back of the house behind that deck somewhere, or do I have to traipse the bike through the house? Check repair issues, permissions, and last sale prices/history. (2026-07-11)

Roof: the listing text says nothing about roof condition either way — can't confirm or rule out what was spotted in the photos from the description alone. Genuinely needs eyes-on or a direct question to the agent, especially given Grade II status limits what repairs are straightforward/permitted. Parking: confirmed on-street only, nothing off-street mentioned anywhere in the listing. What's behind it / bike access: the listing only describes internal access — "the recently installed kitchen enjoys direct access to the garden" — with wooden steps up to a raised deck. No side gate, path, or external route is mentioned anywhere, and no shed/outbuilding is mentioned in the listing at all. Read at face value, a bike stored back there would go out through the kitchen, not around the side — but agents routinely leave out side-access details that exist in reality, so treat this as unconfirmed rather than definitively no side gate, until a viewing. Sale history: Land Registry has entries for other numbered addresses in the same cluster (2 Church Stile Cottages sold £270k in 2007; 3 Church Stile Cottages shows a logged 2026 sale of £657k, which looks like a likely data error given everything else on the lane — treat with caution) but nothing tying definitively to this exact cottage since the listing doesn't give a house number/name. Repairs/permissions: no planning applications, enforcement notices, or repair-related records found for this address — the only nearby planning activity on the lane is routine tree-pruning consent for 3 Church Stile Cottages, unrelated to structure or roof. Bottom line: nothing here rules it out, but the roof and rear-access questions genuinely can't be answered from the listing alone — worth putting directly to the agent before going further.

Research findings

Asked: What is the parking situation like near Queen Street, Budleigh Salterton? (2026-07-19)

Budleigh Salterton does not appear to run a residents-permit on-street scheme the way Sidmouth does — no record of one turned up for the town, including Queen Street specifically. What the town has instead: 5 council car parks with 123 free and 505 pay-and-display spaces between them, all a short walk from the town centre (Queen Street sits right in the middle of town, close to the High Street). Queen Street itself has some on-street bays, consistent with the listing’s “on-street parking only.” Practically: no guaranteed space at the door, but genuinely easy walk-to-parking rather than a real scarcity problem — this is a town-centre-convenience trade-off, not a car-storage crisis.

Research findings

Asked: Sweep re-check: price and any new material disclosures (2026-07-30)

Reduced again on 27 July 2026, from a £250,000 guide to offers in excess of £230,000 — a £20,000 cut, and the second reduction on this cottage. Stags' current listing also now carries a disclosure that was not on the version originally captured: Japanese Knotweed was found at the bottom of the garden in spring 2026. A 10-year insurance-backed treatment guarantee is in place, which is what most lenders require before they will lend, but it is a material fact for both the survey and the resale conversation and should be raised with the agent directly rather than taken as fully closed. Everything else is unchanged — Grade II listed, freehold, one bedroom with an ensuite, inglenook with a log-effect gas stove, substantial south-facing garden with the detached oak-framed garden studio, on-street parking to the front only.

Research findings

Asked: Look further into what you actually do for parking on The Strand, Lympstone. (2026-07-08)

The Strand itself has no dedicated resident bays — parking there is on-street with no confirmed residents' zone. Two car parks serve the immediate area: the free Lympstone Village Station car park right on The Strand (13 spaces, no permit needed, first-come-first-served, but can fill up with rail commuters), and Underhill Car Park a short walk away. Underhill's management has been unsettled for a while — East Devon District Council was in talks with Lympstone Parish Council years ago about the Parish taking it over and potentially issuing permits, and I couldn't confirm what, if anything, was finalised or whether a strict residents' scheme runs there now. Beyond that, East Devon District Council sells modular monthly/annual town permits for its pay-and-display car parks generally, but I couldn't confirm Lympstone is one of the towns those permits cover, nor find a price. Devon County Council handles on-street residents' permit zones separately and I couldn't confirm one exists for The Strand either. Bottom line: there's workable free/cheap parking nearby (the station car park is the best bet), but nothing deeded to the property and nothing guaranteed — worth a direct call to Lympstone Parish Council or East Devon's parking team before relying on it.

Sources: Lympstone Village Website — Underhill Car Park · East Devon District Council — Car park permits · Devon County Council — Residents' parking permits
